chapter: Offers, Earl Foster and Fats Waller
title: Fats Waller at the Lyric Theater and as a pianist
summary: Fats came to the Lyric Theater and sat in; Handy says he had a good six-piece band and played much real piano behind the clowning, then turns to young players.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Well, how did Fat Wallace know you? Fat used to come down here often.
Yeah, Fat used to come here to the Lyric Theater. When I was waiting for Beansy. Sure, Fat used to come over there and sit in and play with us a lot of times.
Yeah, he used to come in there a lot of times. But was he good in a band?
I mean as a band piano player, when he played with the Auditor. Sure.
Yeah, he was a fine man in a band.

Matter of fact, he had a good band. Yeah, I think he had six pieces there, it was wonderful. Because they used to come down here often, they'd play on the stage, you know. Of course he'd do his acting and things like that. But come down to the actual playing, he could play a lot of piano. Fat was a good musician. He'd just do that clowning and singing and going. But he could play nothing. Sit outside and think he couldn't play. Play a lot of piano. Often wondering why the youngsters these days don't like to play the type of music that we played years ago. All they want to play is rock and roll. And if you take that away from them, they can't even feel their home. I remember, you know, it was about four months ago. A trumpet player of ours got sick out there in Bay St. Louis. And went and got one of the little rock and roll trumpet players. And that guy come in there playing. He was trying to play this progressive music. Running all over his home. Kind of like a run over boat running. Running so far out of the key. I thought he was going overboard that war. Couldn't play a waltz. Play a waltz and he have to hold his hand, hold his horn in his hand. Listen. Couldn't get in there. If he got in there, he wanted to play that. Oh Lord.
